body_html:
Video calls with family in Spanish are where many learners use their Spanish most, and where they feel most nervous. The call with your partner’s grandparents in Guadalajara, or with cousins in Bogotá, mixes small talk, family news and the inevitable tech problems. The good news is that these calls follow a predictable pattern: greetings, checking the connection, catching up, and a long, warm goodbye. Learn the phrases for each part and the call becomes much easier.

Quick answer
  • Start: ¡Hola! ¿Me ven? ¿Me escuchan?
  • Tech problems: Se congeló la imagen. Se te corta.
  • Catching up: ¿Cómo han estado? ¿Qué hay de nuevo?
  • Goodbye: Les mando un abrazo. ¡Cuídense mucho!
{{toc}}

Starting video calls with family in Spanish

SpanishEnglish
¡Hola! ¿Me ves? ¿Me escuchas?Hi! Can you see me? Can you hear me?
¡Hola a todos!Hi, everyone!
¡Qué gusto verlos!It’s so nice to see you all!
¿Cómo están?How are you all?
¿Cómo ha estado, abuela?How have you been, Grandma? (formal)
Te ves muy bien.You look great.

Notice the plural ustedes forms (están, verlos) when several people are on screen. With grandparents and older relatives you may use usted, depending on the family; see {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.

When the technology fails

SpanishEnglish
No te escucho.I can’t hear you.
Se te corta.You’re breaking up.
Se congeló la imagen.The picture froze.
Tienes el micrófono apagado.Your microphone is off.
Prende la cámara.Turn on your camera. (Latin America; Spain: Enciende la cámara)
Acércate un poco a la pantalla.Move a bit closer to the screen.
Te marco otra vez.I’ll call you again. (Mexico)
Se cayó la llamada.The call dropped.

With older relatives, a gentle No se preocupe, ya le marco otra vez (Don’t worry, I’ll call you back) saves a lot of stress on both sides.

{{image:2}}

Catching up with family news

  • ¿Qué hay de nuevo? What’s new?
  • ¿Cómo sigue tu papá? How is your dad doing? (after an illness)
  • ¿Cómo les fue en la fiesta? How did the party go?
  • Los niños ya están enormes. The kids are so big now.
  • Aquí todo bien, gracias a Dios. All good here, thank God.
  • Les cuento que… I wanted to tell you that…

Gracias a Dios is very common in Mexican and Central American families, even among people who aren’t especially religious. You will hear it often, and it is fine to say it back.

Talking with grandparents

Calls with grandparents are often the most important and the most challenging, because they may speak quickly, use regional words or have trouble with the technology. A few habits help:

  • Ask simple, open questions: ¿Qué cocinó hoy? (What did you cook today?) ¿Cómo está su salud? (How is your health?)
  • Show you are listening: ¿De veras? ¡Qué bueno! Ay, qué pena.
  • Ask them to slow down kindly: ¿Me lo repite más despacio, por favor?
  • Share something small: a photo, a meal you made, a drawing by the kids.

Grandparents rarely care about your grammar. They care that you are trying. For more on building that relationship, see {{link:talking-to-your-in-laws-in-spanish|talking to your in-laws in Spanish}}.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

A sample family call

Abuela: ¿Bueno? ¿Me escuchas, mijo?
Hello? Can you hear me, dear?

Mike: ¡Sí, abuela! Ahora sí la escucho. ¿Cómo ha estado?
Yes, Grandma! Now I can hear you. How have you been?

Abuela: Bien, bien, gracias a Dios. ¿Y los niños?
Good, good, thank God. And the kids?

Mike: Están aquí. ¡Niños, vengan a saludar a la abuela!
They’re here. Kids, come say hi to Grandma!

Abuela: ¡Ay, qué grandes están!
Oh, how big they are!

Mijo and mija (from mi hijo, mi hija) are affectionate words that Mexican grandparents use for children and grandchildren.

Calls with kids on both sides

When children are on the call, keep it short and visual. Ask them to show something: ¿Me enseñas tu dibujo? (Will you show me your drawing?) ¿Qué hiciste en la escuela? (What did you do at school?) Children in bilingual families often answer in English, and that is fine. Keep speaking Spanish warmly and let them hear it; see {{link:talking-to-kids-in-spanish|talking to kids in Spanish}}.

{{image:3}}

Saying goodbye

Goodbyes in Spanish-speaking families can take a while, and rushing them can feel cold. These phrases help you close warmly:

  • Bueno, los dejo. Well, I’ll let you go.
  • Les mando un abrazo muy fuerte. Sending you all a big hug.
  • Saludos a todos por allá. Say hi to everyone there.
  • ¡Cuídense mucho! Take good care of yourselves!
  • Hablamos el domingo, ¿sí? Let’s talk on Sunday, okay?
  • Los quiero mucho. I love you all.

Expect several rounds of cuídense, besos and bye before anyone actually hangs up. For phone calls without video, see {{link:phone-calls-in-spanish|phone calls in Spanish}}, and if someone you miss lives far away, {{link:how-to-say-i-miss-you-in-spanish|how to say I miss you in Spanish}}.

If you want to check a regional word a relative used, the Diccionario de la lengua española marks many words by country.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Video calls with family in Spanish get easier every week. Learn the tech phrases once, prepare two or three questions before each call, and let the conversation flow from there. Your relatives will remember the effort far more than any mistakes. For other everyday moments, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say “Can you hear me?” in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Me escuchas? or ¿Me oyes? to one person, and ¿Me escuchan? to several.

faq.q: How do I say “You’re breaking up” in Spanish?
faq.a: Se te corta or Se te está cortando la llamada.

faq.q: Should I use tú or usted with my partner’s grandparents?
faq.a: Follow the family’s lead. Many families use usted with grandparents; start formal and switch if they invite you.
It is short for mi hijo (my son) and is used affectionately for children, grandchildren and even younger adults.

questions.explain: Se te corta is the natural phrase for a bad connection.
Congelarse is used for a frozen screen.

questions.q: To several relatives: “How are you all?”
questions.explain: In Latin America, ustedes is the plural for everyone.
It comes from mi hija and is very affectionate.
